intro: Sport runs on categories and on public support. A governing body decides who may enter the women's race, which Paralympic class an athlete belongs in, and what evidence settles a dispute. A city council or state legislature decides whether taxes pay for a stadium and whether homes can be taken to clear land for it.

This unit follows both kinds of decision through real cases. You will read about the Women's World Games of 1922, chromosome tests from 1968, the Semenya and Pistorius cases at the Court of Arbitration for Sport, and the Sydney 2000 ban. You will also trace Soldier Field, the Illinois Sports Facilities Authority, Chavez Ravine, the Colts' move and the tax code.

By the end you will be able to name who wrote a rule, what evidence it used, who it let in or shut out, and which court or vote tested it. You will also be able to weigh a public stadium deal using what economists measured, and build an argument from dated records instead of slogans.
bigQuestion: Who gets to decide which bodies count in sport and how much the public pays for it, and how can those decisions be challenged?

title: Bodies, Data, and the State

chapters.title: Classification, Sex, and Eligibility
chapters.bigQuestion: When a sports body sorts athletes into categories, whose evidence decides which box a person belongs in, and who can challenge it?

story.title: A Box on a Form
story.kicker: Every entry form asks an athlete to fit a category, and the category was written by a governing body.
paragraphs: An entry form for an international track meet asks for a name, a nation, an event and a category. The category line looks simple. Yet the words behind it, women's or men's, open or classified, were written by a governing body. Those bodies have rewritten them many times since the 1920s.

Some categories exist to open doors. Women's events were added to the Olympic track program in 1928 only after women organized their own games. Paralympic classes exist so that athletes with different impairments can compete against others with similar ones. Without those boxes, many athletes would have had no place to enter at all.

Every box also has an edge, and someone has to decide who stands on which side. Since 1966, track officials have used physical inspections, chromosome tests and hormone limits to police the women's category. Paralympic officials have used medical files and observation. Each method has been challenged, and several have been dropped.

This chapter follows those rules as institutions. It asks who wrote each rule, what evidence it used, which athletes it shut out or let in, and which court or panel heard the appeal. The goal is to describe a live argument accurately, with names and dates, not to settle it with a slogan.
story.think: Why might a category that opens a door for one group of athletes also create a new question about who belongs inside it?

lessons.title: Women at the Early Olympics
lessons.mainIdea: Women entered the modern Olympics in 1900, but the IOC kept them out of track and field until 1928.
reading: The first modern Olympics, in Athens in 1896, had no events for women. Pierre de Coubertin, the French founder of the *International Olympic Committee* (IOC), opposed women competing in public. At the 1900 Paris Games women entered a few sports, including tennis and golf. Charlotte Cooper of Britain won the tennis singles and became the first woman to win an Olympic event.

Track and field, the center of the Games, stayed closed to women for three more decades. The sport's world body, the International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF), was founded in 1912 and ran only men's events at first. Swimming added women's races in 1912 in Stockholm. Each federation decided on its own whether women had a *category* in its sport.

Women's track events finally appeared at the 1928 Amsterdam Games, with five events. After the 800 meters, newspapers claimed that runners had collapsed, and officials dropped the race. Women did not run an Olympic 800 meters again until 1960 in Rome. The story shows how a category could be opened and closed by the same officials within one Games.

words.d: the body founded in 1894 that runs the Olympic Games and decides which sports and events they include
a group, such as women's or men's, that a sports body sets up so that only certain athletes compete against each other
the world governing body for one sport, which writes that sport's rules and entry standards

lessons.title: Milliat's Women's Games
lessons.mainIdea: When the IOC refused women's track events, Alice Milliat built a separate women's federation and its own world games.
reading: Alice Milliat was a French rower and sports organizer. In 1919 she asked the IOC to add women's track and field to the 1920 Games, and it refused. In 1921 she and others founded the *Fédération Sportive Féminine Internationale* (FSFI), an international federation run for women's sport. It set its own records and rules.

In August 1922 the FSFI held the first *Women's World Games* in Paris. Athletes from five nations, including the United States and Britain, competed before a large crowd in a single day. More Women's World Games followed in Gothenburg in 1926, Prague in 1930 and London in 1934. The IAAF objected at first to the FSFI using the word Olympic.

The separate games put pressure on the IAAF and IOC. A rival body with its own records threatened their control of the sport. The IAAF agreed to a small women's program for 1928, and by the mid-1930s it took over women's records. The FSFI then faded and dissolved. The case shows a shut-out group building a *parallel* institution to force a door open.

words.d: the international women's sports federation founded in 1921 by Alice Milliat and others
international women's track meets held by the FSFI from 1922 to 1934
running side by side, as a separate institution built by people shut out of an older one

lessons.title: A Marathon Without Women
lessons.mainIdea: Road races and the Olympics kept women out of the marathon for decades; Boston admitted women in 1972 and the Olympics in 1984.
reading: The Boston Marathon, first run in 1897, had no category for women. In 1966 Roberta Gibb ran it without a number after hiding near the start. In 1967 Kathrine Switzer entered as K. V. Switzer and received an official *bib*, the numbered cloth runners wear. A race official tried to pull her number off during the race, and photographs of the scene spread worldwide.

The Amateur Athletic Union, which then governed American distance running, barred women from races longer than a few miles. Runners and organizers pushed back through the late 1960s. In 1972 the Boston Marathon officially opened a women's division. Nina Kuscsik won it that first year. The rule change came from the race and the national body, not from the runners' fitness.

The IOC added a women's Olympic marathon for the 1984 Los Angeles Games. Joan Benoit of Maine won it. The women's 10,000 meters did not join the Olympics until 1988 in Seoul. These dates show that the women's category grew event by event, each through a vote by a *governing body*.

words.d: the numbered cloth a registered runner wears, proof of an official entry
the body founded in 1888 that governed much of American amateur sport, including road running
an organization that writes the rules and decides who may enter a sport's events

lessons.title: Inspections and Chromosomes
lessons.mainIdea: From 1966 track officials checked women athletes' bodies, and from 1968 the IOC used a chromosome test.
reading: In the Cold War years, some Western officials and newspapers claimed that men were entering women's events. Historians have found little evidence for that claim. Even so, at the 1966 European Championships in Budapest, the IAAF required women to pass a physical inspection by doctors. Many athletes later described the checks as humiliating. The inspections were a new kind of *eligibility* rule.

In 1968 the IOC replaced inspections with a laboratory test. The *Barr body test* looked at cells scraped from inside the cheek for a sign of two X chromosomes. It was used at the Winter Games in Grenoble and the Summer Games in Mexico City. Women who passed received a certificate so they would not need to be tested again.

Geneticists soon pointed out problems. Some women have chromosome patterns that differ from the typical XX, yet their bodies gain no athletic advantage from it. Such natural variations are now often called *differences of sex development* (DSD). A test built on one marker could shut out women who had lived as women their whole lives.

words.d: the rules for who is allowed to enter a competition or category
a chromosome test from cheek cells, used by the IOC to screen women athletes from 1968
natural variations in chromosomes, hormones or anatomy; often shortened to DSD

lessons.title: Martínez-Patiño Appeals
lessons.mainIdea: Spanish hurdler María José Martínez-Patiño challenged a failed chromosome test in 1985 and was reinstated.
reading: María José Martínez-Patiño was a Spanish hurdler. At the 1985 World University Games in Kobe, Japan, she failed the chromosome screen. Tests showed she had a Y chromosome and *androgen insensitivity*, a condition in which the body cannot respond to testosterone. She had lived as a woman all her life and did not know of the condition.

Spanish officials told her to fake an injury and withdraw quietly. She refused. News of the result became public, and she lost her place on the national team, her records and her scholarship. She then worked with geneticist Albert de la Chapelle and others to show that her condition gave her no advantage. In 1988 the IAAF restored her *eligibility*.

Her case helped end universal screening. The IAAF stopped testing every woman in the early 1990s. In 1999 the IOC voted to drop routine sex testing before the 2000 Sydney Games. From then on, officials could still examine an athlete whose eligibility was questioned. That shift moved sex testing from a gate for everyone to a *case-by-case* review.

words.d: a condition in which the body cannot respond to testosterone and related hormones
to restore someone's right to compete after a ban
handled one athlete at a time when a question is raised, instead of testing everyone

lessons.title: Testosterone Limits and Court
lessons.mainIdea: Since 2011 track's governing body has used testosterone limits for women, and athletes have fought them at CAS and in European courts.
reading: In 2011 the IAAF introduced *hyperandrogenism* rules. Hyperandrogenism means naturally high levels of testosterone. Women above a set limit had to lower their levels to compete. Indian sprinter Dutee Chand was barred under the rules and appealed to the *Court of Arbitration for Sport* (CAS), a tribunal in Lausanne, Switzerland, that hears sports disputes.

In July 2015 CAS suspended the IAAF rules. The panel said the IAAF had not shown enough evidence that natural testosterone gave a large advantage. The IAAF then wrote new rules in 2018 that applied only to events from 400 meters to the mile. South African runner Caster Semenya, a two-time Olympic 800 meters champion, challenged them.

In 2019 CAS ruled against Semenya, calling the rules discriminatory but necessary. The Swiss Federal Supreme Court upheld that ruling in 2020. Semenya then took her case to the *European Court of Human Rights*, which ruled in her favor on procedural grounds in July 2023. World Athletics, the IAAF's new name, extended its limits to all women's events that year.

a tribunal in Lausanne, Switzerland, founded in 1984, that decides disputes in international sport
a court in Strasbourg, France, that hears claims that a European state violated the European Convention on Human Rights
the name the IAAF adopted in 2019 for track and field's world governing body

lessons.title: Transgender Athlete Policies
lessons.mainIdea: IOC rules for transgender athletes changed in 2004, 2015 and 2021, and each federation now writes its own.
reading: A *transgender* person has a gender identity different from the sex recorded at birth. In 2004 the IOC adopted the Stockholm Consensus. It allowed transgender athletes to compete after surgery, legal recognition and two years of hormone therapy. Few athletes met all three conditions, and critics said the surgery rule had no link to performance.

In November 2015 the IOC issued new guidelines. They dropped the surgery requirement. Transgender women could enter women's events if their testosterone stayed below 10 nanomoles per liter for at least twelve months. The guidelines were advice to federations, not binding rules, and federations applied them in different ways.

In November 2021 the IOC published its *Framework on Fairness, Inclusion and Non-Discrimination*. It said no athlete should be presumed to have an advantage and handed eligibility decisions to each sport's federation. In 2023 World Athletics barred transgender women who had gone through male puberty from the women's category. Swimming's federation had adopted a similar rule in 2022, so rules now differ from sport to sport.

words.d: having a gender identity different from the sex recorded at birth
the IOC's 2004 rules for transgender athletes, which required surgery, legal recognition and hormone therapy
a set of principles that guides rule makers without writing every rule itself

lessons.title: Sydney 2000 and a Ban
lessons.mainIdea: After a Spanish team broke eligibility rules at Sydney 2000, the IPC removed athletes with intellectual impairments until 2012.
reading: At the 2000 Sydney Paralympics, Spain won the gold medal in basketball for athletes with an *intellectual impairment*. That term means a significant limit in thinking and learning skills that appears in childhood. Soon after, a Spanish journalist, Carlos Ribagorda, revealed that he had played on the team. He said most of the players had never been tested and had no impairment.

Spain's sports officials investigated and confirmed the fraud. The team returned its medals. The *International Paralympic Committee* (IPC), the world body for the Paralympics, then suspended all events for athletes with intellectual impairments. It said it needed a reliable way to check eligibility before those athletes could return.

The ban lasted more than a decade and shut out many honest athletes. The IPC worked with the international federation for athletes with intellectual impairments, now called Virtus, to build new tests. Athletes with intellectual impairments returned at the London 2012 Paralympics in three sports: athletics, swimming and table tennis. The case shows how one fraud closed a category for everyone in it.

the world governing body for the Paralympic Games, founded in 1989
deliberate cheating by giving false information

lessons.title: Pistorius and the Open Track
lessons.mainIdea: In 2008 CAS overturned a ban on Oscar Pistorius's prosthetic legs, and he ran in the 2012 Olympics.
reading: Oscar Pistorius was a South African sprinter who ran on carbon-fiber *prosthetic* legs, artificial limbs built for running. He won Paralympic gold in 2004. He then tried to qualify for the Olympics against runners without disabilities. In 2007 the IAAF added a rule against devices that give a runner an advantage over one not using them.

In January 2008 the IAAF ruled Pistorius ineligible, citing a study it had paid for. He appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport. In May 2008 CAS overturned the ban. The panel said the IAAF had not proven that the prosthetics gave him an overall advantage over a whole race. The ruling put the *burden of proof* on the governing body.

Pistorius ran the 400 meters and the 4 x 400 meters relay at the London 2012 Olympics, the first double-leg amputee to run on an Olympic track. He then raced at the London Paralympics weeks later. In 2013 he killed Reeva Steenkamp at his home, and South African courts later convicted him of her murder. His eligibility case remains a legal precedent even though his name is now tied to that crime.

words.d: an artificial body part, such as a leg, made to replace a missing limb
the duty of one side in a dispute to prove its claim
an earlier decision that later panels and courts look to in similar cases

lessons.title: A Code for Classification
lessons.mainIdea: In 2007 the IPC adopted an Athlete Classification Code so that sorting athletes rests on written rules and research.
reading: Early Paralympic sport sorted athletes by medical diagnosis, such as spinal cord injury or amputation. Each disability group ran its own classes, so one Games could have many small events. In the 1990s the IPC began moving toward *functional classification*. That system groups athletes by how an impairment affects a particular sport, not by the name of the diagnosis.

In November 2007 the IPC General Assembly approved the *IPC Athlete Classification Code*. It set shared rules for all Paralympic sports. It listed which impairments are eligible, required trained classifiers, and gave athletes a right to protest a class. A revised Code took effect in 2015 and called for classification to be *evidence-based*, tied to research on each sport.

Classification disputes still reach the news. Athletes and coaches have argued that some rivals were placed in classes with less severe impairments. Other athletes have lost their eligibility after a review and ended careers. The Code gives these disputes a written process, with protests and appeals, instead of leaving them to a single official's judgment.

words.d: grouping athletes by how an impairment affects a sport, not by medical diagnosis
the IPC's shared classification rules, adopted in 2007 and revised in 2015
built on research data rather than on custom or opinion
in classification, a formal request to review an athlete's class

chapters.title: The State in the Stadium
chapters.bigQuestion: When governments build stadiums, take land, grant tax breaks and run the schools where athletes train, what do the public and the teams each owe the other?

story.title: Lights on a Public Bond
story.kicker: A stadium owned by the public can pay for the lights that a private team uses on Sunday.
paragraphs: On a Sunday in autumn, the lights come on over Soldier Field on Chicago's lakefront. The Chicago Bears, a private company, play there. The building belongs to the Chicago Park District, a public body. Its 2003 rebuilding was paid for with bonds sold by a state agency and repaid from a tax on hotel rooms.

A *bond* is a loan that a government takes from investors and pays back over many years with interest. Visitors who never see a game pay part of the hotel tax. The team pays rent and keeps most of its ticket, television and sponsorship money. The deal was set by state law, not by a vote of the fans.

Chicago is one example among many. Across the United States, cities and states have paid for arenas, taken homes to clear land, written tax rules for leagues, and trained future professionals in public high schools. Each of these choices was made by legislators, courts, voters or school boards on a particular date.

This chapter looks at the government's hand in sport. It follows public money, public land and public schools into the business of professional teams. It asks what each deal promised, who paid, who was moved, and what economists later measured.
story.think: If the public pays for a building that a private team uses, what should the public receive in return?

lessons.title: A Lakefront Stadium, 1924
lessons.mainIdea: Soldier Field was built by a public park board in the 1920s, decades before a professional team made it home.
reading: In the early 1920s Chicago's South Park Commission, a public park board, built a stadium on the lakefront south of Grant Park. It opened in 1924 as Municipal Grant Park Stadium. In 1925 it was renamed Soldier Field to honor Americans who died in the First World War. It was paid for with public money raised by the park board.

For decades the stadium served as a *civic* space, meaning one used by the whole city. It hosted the 1927 boxing rematch between Jack Dempsey and Gene Tunney, high school football championships, religious gatherings and the first Special Olympics Summer Games in 1968. The Chicago Park District, formed in 1934 from twenty-two park boards, took over the building.

The Chicago Bears moved to Soldier Field in 1971 from Wrigley Field. From then on a private National Football League club became the stadium's main *tenant*, a renter who uses a building owned by someone else. The Bears paid rent to the Park District. Questions about who should pay for repairs and upgrades grew over the next thirty years.

words.d: belonging to or used by the whole city and its people
a renter who uses a building owned by someone else
the public body, formed in 1934, that owns and runs Chicago's parks and Soldier Field

lessons.title: A State Authority for Stadiums
lessons.mainIdea: In 1987 Illinois created a state agency to build a new White Sox park, and it later financed the Soldier Field rebuild.
reading: By the 1980s Comiskey Park, opened in 1910, was the oldest park in the major leagues. The White Sox owners wanted a new one and talked with officials in St. Petersburg, Florida, about moving there. In 1987 the Illinois General Assembly created the *Illinois Sports Facilities Authority* (ISFA), a state agency with the power to build and own stadiums.

In the summer of 1988 legislators approved money for a new park in a vote held late at night, just as a deadline passed. The ISFA sold bonds to build it, repaid largely with a tax on Chicago hotel rooms. New Comiskey Park opened in 1991 across 35th Street from the old one, which was torn down. The White Sox became its tenant.

In 2001 the state gave the ISFA another job: rebuilding Soldier Field for the Bears. The project kept the old columns and set a new bowl inside them, reopening in 2003. The ISFA again sold bonds backed by the hotel tax. A *public authority*, an agency set up by law for one purpose, let the state borrow for sport outside its regular budget.

words.d: a state agency created in 1987 to build and own sports venues in Chicago
a loan a government takes from investors and repays over many years with interest
a government agency created by law to do one job, such as building stadiums
a tax added to the price of a hotel room, paid mostly by visitors

check.why: The owners talked with St. Petersburg, Florida, about a move.

choices: A tax on Chicago hotel rooms
check.why: The bonds were repaid largely with a tax on Chicago hotel rooms.

lessons.title: A Private Arena Next Door
lessons.mainIdea: The United Center, opened in 1994, was built with the owners' money, a contrast to Chicago's two ballparks.
reading: Chicago Stadium opened on West Madison Street in 1929. It was home to the Blackhawks hockey club and the Bulls basketball club. By the late 1980s its owners wanted a larger arena with more premium seats. Jerry Reinsdorf of the Bulls and Bill Wirtz of the Blackhawks formed a *joint venture*, a business shared by two owners, to build one.

The United Center opened across the street in 1994, and Chicago Stadium was torn down the next year. The owners paid for construction with private loans rather than public bonds. The owners, not taxpayers, carried the construction debt. The arena name was sold to United Airlines as *naming rights*.

The contrast shows that public funding was a choice, not a rule. Reinsdorf also owned the White Sox, whose park was built by the state authority three years earlier. The same owner used public money for one building and private money for another. The difference depended on what each city and state offered and what each team could threaten.

words.d: a business project owned and run together by two or more partners
the right, sold for money, to put a company's name on a building
higher-priced seats and private boxes that bring extra income to a venue's owner

look.title: Two Buildings, One Owner
look.text: In 1991 a baseball park opens on the South Side, built by a state agency with bonds. In 1994 an arena opens on the West Side, built by two team owners with private loans. One of those owners holds a stake in both buildings.
look.prompt: What might explain why one project used public money and the other did not? What would you want to know about each deal?

choices: The Bears and the White Sox
check.why: The Bulls and Blackhawks owners built the arena as a joint venture.

check.q: How was the United Center mainly financed?
check.why: The owners paid with private loans, unlike the ISFA's bond-funded parks.

choices: The right, sold for money, to name a building

lessons.title: Chavez Ravine, 1950–1962
lessons.mainIdea: Los Angeles cleared the Mexican American neighborhoods of Chavez Ravine for housing that was never built, then gave the land to the Dodgers.
reading: Chavez Ravine, near downtown Los Angeles, held three mostly Mexican American neighborhoods: La Loma, Palo Verde and Bishop. In 1950 the city's housing authority planned a large public housing project there. It used *eminent domain*, the government's power to take private land for public use with payment, to buy out and remove hundreds of families.

In 1953, after a political fight and a new mayor, the city canceled the housing plan. Most homes had already been cleared. In 1957 the city offered the land to Walter O'Malley to bring his Brooklyn Dodgers west. Opponents forced a *referendum*, a public vote on a law. In June 1958 voters approved the contract, Proposition B, by a narrow margin.

A few families had stayed on the land. In May 1959 sheriff's deputies carried members of the Aréchiga family out of their home as television cameras filmed. Dodger Stadium opened in April 1962. The story remains a lasting memory in Mexican American Los Angeles, and it shows how land taken for one public purpose was later handed to a private team.

words.d: the government's power to take private land for public use, as long as it pays the owner
a public vote in which citizens approve or reject a law or contract
forcing people to leave their homes and neighborhood

look.title: One Hillside, Two Plans
look.text: 1950: the city says the land will become public housing for working families, and residents must sell. 1953: the housing plan is canceled. 1957: the city offers the same land to a baseball club moving from Brooklyn. 1958: voters narrowly approve the deal.
look.prompt: Was the land still being used for a public purpose in 1957? How might a family who sold in 1951 see the 1958 vote?

check.q: Why did Los Angeles first clear Chavez Ravine around 1950?
check.why: The housing authority planned public housing, which was canceled in 1953.

check.q: What is a referendum?
choices: A court order to leave a home
A contract signed by a team owner
A public vote on a law or contract
check.why: In 1958 voters approved the Dodgers contract in a referendum, Proposition B.

check.q: When did Dodger Stadium open?
check.why: Dodger Stadium opened in April 1962.

lessons.title: Public Use and the Courts
lessons.mainIdea: The Supreme Court's 2005 Kelo decision widened public use, and a New York court applied that reasoning to Brooklyn's arena land.
reading: The Fifth Amendment to the Constitution says private property shall not be taken for *public use* without just compensation. For a long time, public use meant roads, schools or parks. Over the twentieth century courts allowed takings for urban renewal, the clearing of neighborhoods officials labeled as blighted. *Blight* is a legal label for an area judged run-down or unsafe.

In Kelo v. City of New London, decided in 2005, the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4 that a city could take homes for a private economic development plan. The majority said the plan served a public purpose. Justice Sandra Day O'Connor, in dissent, warned that any property could now be taken for a richer private use. Many states then passed laws to limit such takings.

In Brooklyn, a New York State agency used eminent domain to assemble land for the Atlantic Yards project, which included an arena for the Nets. Residents sued, and in 2009 New York's highest court, the Court of Appeals, upheld the taking in Goldstein v. New York State Urban Development Corporation. The Barclays Center opened on the site in 2012.

words.d: the Fifth Amendment's condition for taking private land; courts have read it broadly as public purpose
a legal label for an area officials judge to be run-down, often used to justify taking land
the fair payment the Constitution requires when government takes property

look.title: A Warning in Dissent
look.text: Justice O'Connor wrote that under the majority's reasoning, nothing would stop the government from replacing a small home with a shopping mall, or a family farm with a factory, so long as officials believed the new use would bring more benefit.
look.cite: Kelo v. City of New London, 545 U.S. 469 (2005), O'Connor, J., dissenting
look.prompt: How might O'Connor's warning apply to land taken for an arena? What would a city say in reply?

check.q: Which amendment says property may not be taken for public use without just compensation?
check.why: The Fifth Amendment sets the public use and just compensation rule.

check.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in Kelo v. City of New London in 2005?
choices: A city could take homes for a private development plan
check.why: The Court ruled 5 to 4 that the development plan served a public purpose.

check.q: Which arena opened on land assembled with eminent domain in Brooklyn?
check.why: The Barclays Center opened in 2012 on the Atlantic Yards site.

lessons.title: A League Office Without Taxes
lessons.mainIdea: In 1966 Congress wrote professional football leagues into a tax exemption, and the NFL gave it up in 2015.
reading: In 1966 the National Football League and the American Football League agreed to merge. The merger needed help from Congress, because antitrust law, which bans companies from combining to limit competition, could block it. That year Congress passed a law allowing the merger. The same law changed section 501(c)(6) of the tax code to list *professional football leagues*.

Section 501(c)(6) covers business leagues and trade associations, such as chambers of commerce. Groups under it do not pay federal income tax on their dues. The change meant the NFL's league office, which collected dues from its clubs, was *tax-exempt*. The thirty-two clubs themselves always paid taxes on their profits.

Critics in Congress argued that a league earning billions from television should not enjoy a nonprofit status. In April 2015 NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell announced that the league office would give up its exemption. The NHL and the PGA Tour had also used the same section of the tax code. The case shows a sports rule written directly into federal law.

words.d: laws that stop companies from combining or agreeing in ways that limit competition
not required to pay a particular tax under the law
the joining of two businesses or leagues into one

look.title: Club Versus League Office
look.text: A club in the league sells tickets, pays players and reports its profit to the tax authorities. The league office collects dues from all the clubs, negotiates rules and runs the championship. From 1966 to 2015 the first paid federal income tax and the second did not.
look.prompt: Why might Congress have treated the league office like a trade association? Why did critics disagree?

check.q: Why did the 1966 NFL and AFL merger need Congress?
choices: Leagues must be licensed by Congress
Television was owned by the government
check.why: Antitrust law bans combinations that limit competition, so Congress passed a law allowing the merger.

check.q: What does tax-exempt mean?
choices: Not required to pay a particular tax
check.why: The league office did not pay federal income tax on its dues.

check.q: When did the NFL announce its league office would give up the exemption?
check.why: Commissioner Roger Goodell announced the change in April 2015.

lessons.title: The Colts Leave at Night
lessons.mainIdea: In March 1984 the Baltimore Colts moved to Indianapolis overnight, as Maryland tried to seize the team by eminent domain.
reading: The Colts had played in Baltimore since 1953. Owner Robert Irsay wanted a new stadium and weighed offers from other cities. Indianapolis had built the Hoosier Dome, a covered stadium paid for with public money, without a team to fill it. In March 1984 the Maryland legislature moved to give Baltimore the power to take the team by eminent domain.

Before that law could be used, Irsay acted. On the night of March 28–29, 1984, moving vans carried the team's equipment and offices out of Baltimore in a snowstorm. By morning the Colts were headed for Indianapolis. The city then sued to take the team, but courts ruled that the club had already left Maryland's reach.

The move became a symbol of *relocation*, a team leaving one city for another. Baltimore lost NFL football until 1996, when the Cleveland Browns moved there and became the Ravens. That deal also depended on a new stadium paid largely with public money. Cities learned that a team's threat to leave was a powerful bargaining tool.

words.d: a team moving from one city to another
the publicly funded covered stadium in Indianapolis that opened in 1984
the bargaining power that comes from being able to walk away

lessons.title: What Economists Found
lessons.mainIdea: Economists who studied stadium deals in the 1990s found little evidence that they increased local income or jobs.
reading: Team owners and city officials often promised that a new stadium would bring jobs, tourism and growth. In 1997 economists Roger Noll and Andrew Zimbalist published *Sports, Jobs, and Taxes* through the Brookings Institution. The book collected studies of stadium projects in many cities. Its authors concluded that few if any showed a positive effect on local economic growth.

One reason is *substitution*. A family that spends money on a game usually spends less on movies, restaurants or other outings in the same area. The money moves around inside the region rather than adding to it. Many stadium jobs are also seasonal and part-time, while the players and owners who earn the most often live elsewhere.

Economists do not claim that stadiums have no value. Residents may value a team as a shared civic symbol, a kind of *public good* that people enjoy even without buying tickets. The argument is over price: whether that value is worth the hundreds of millions of public dollars a stadium can cost. Voters and legislators still weigh that question deal by deal.

words.d: spending that moves from one local activity to another instead of adding new money
something many people enjoy at once, whether or not they pay for it
public money given to help a private business or project

look.title: A Study of Stadium Deals
look.text: Noll and Zimbalist concluded that sports facilities have attracted little new spending to their cities and have not been a source of local economic growth or jobs, so their benefits fall short of their public cost.
look.cite: Roger G. Noll and Andrew Zimbalist, eds., Sports, Jobs, and Taxes, Brookings Institution Press, 1997
look.prompt: What evidence would a city need to answer this conclusion? Which reasons from the reading explain it?

check.q: What did Noll and Zimbalist conclude in 1997?
choices: Stadiums showed little effect on local growth
check.why: Their collected studies found few if any positive effects on local growth.

check.q: What is substitution in stadium economics?
choices: Replacing a player during a game

check.why: A family that spends at a game usually spends less elsewhere nearby.

check.q: What do economists say the real argument is about?
choices: Whether a team's value is worth the public cost
check.why: The debate is over price: whether civic value justifies the public dollars.

lessons.title: A Draft Reaches the Schools
lessons.mainIdea: Professional leagues draft players trained in public schools and colleges, and they write their own rules about when.
reading: In the United States, most future professional athletes first played on teams run by public high schools. Coaches, fields and gyms are paid for largely by local property taxes. The National Federation of State High School Associations, formed in 1920 by Midwestern state associations including Illinois, writes playing rules for most high school sports. Professional leagues pay none of these costs.

Major League Baseball held its first *amateur draft* in 1965. A draft is a system in which clubs take turns claiming the right to sign young players. Baseball clubs may draft players straight out of high school. Many then play in the minor leagues, a *farm system* of clubs owned or tied to major league teams, which Branch Rickey built for the St. Louis Cardinals in the 1920s and 1930s.

The National Basketball Association let players enter from high school for years; Kevin Garnett in 1995 and LeBron James in 2003 went straight from school to the NBA. In 2005 the league and its players' union agreed that players must be at least 19 and one year past high school graduation. That *age rule* pushed most top players into one season of college basketball.

words.d: a system in which clubs take turns claiming the right to sign young unpaid players
a chain of minor league clubs that trains players for a major league team
the NBA's 2005 rule that players be 19 and a year past high school before entering the league

rows: National Federation of state associations formed
look.cite: NFHS history; Major League Baseball draft records; NBA collective bargaining agreement, 2005
look.prompt: Which of these rules were written by leagues and which by school bodies? Who pays to train players before the draft?

check.q: When did Major League Baseball hold its first amateur draft?
check.why: Baseball's first amateur draft was held in 1965.

check.q: What did the NBA's 2005 age rule require?

check.why: The 2005 agreement set age 19 and one year past high school.

lessons.title: Club Academies Abroad
lessons.mainIdea: In much of Europe, professional soccer clubs train their own young players in academies, while American teams rely on public schools and colleges.
reading: In many European countries, sport for teenagers is organized by clubs, not schools. Professional soccer clubs run *youth academies* that recruit children, pay coaches and often house players. FC Barcelona opened a residence for young players, La Masia, in 1979. Ajax of Amsterdam built its academy into one of the best-known training systems in the world.

Under that model, the club pays much of the cost of training and in return holds the first right to sign the players it develops. FIFA's transfer rules include *training compensation*, payments that a buying club owes to the clubs that trained a young player. The money flows back toward the institutions that did the training.

In the United States, the training cost falls on public schools, colleges and families. School districts pay coaches and build fields with tax money. Colleges fund teams through tuition, fees and television income. No rule sends a share of a professional contract back to the high school that coached the player. The comparison makes visible the public role that American schools play in professional sport.

words.d: a program run by a professional club to recruit and train young players
FIFA-required payments from a buying club to the clubs that trained a young player
FC Barcelona's residence and academy for young players, opened in 1979

look.title: Two Paths to a Contract
look.text: Player A, in Spain, joins a club academy at age twelve. The club pays her coaches and housing, and when she signs elsewhere, her old club receives a training payment. Player B, in Illinois, plays for her public high school, coached by a teacher paid by the district. When she signs a pro contract, the school receives nothing.
look.prompt: Who paid to train each player? Should any of Player B's future contract go back to her school? Give a reason.

review.q: Why do economists say stadiums add little to local income?
choices: Most fans travel from other states
